hints.addition: Take relative homology of the pair \((X^n,X^{n-1})\) in degree \(n\); the cell interiors supply relative generators after the lower skeleton is collapsed.
Orient each characteristic disk to choose a generator. For infinitely many cells the group is a direct sum of copies of \(\mathbb Z\), not a product.
For \(n\ge2\), compose the attaching sphere with the quotient onto a chosen \((n-1)\)-cell sphere and compute its signed degree; in degree one use terminal minus initial vertex.
The cellular differential lands in \(C_{n-1}^{\mathrm{cell}}(X)\); a zero target forces this map to vanish regardless of the attaching formula.
For \(n\ge1\), distinguish the base zero-cell from the top cell. When \(n=1\), the edge boundary vanishes because its endpoints coincide, not because its target is zero.
Compute both the outgoing kernel and incoming image at the top cell; there are no cells in degree \(n+1\) in the minimal sphere model.
Read the standard square identifications: all corners give one vertex, the opposite edge pairs give two edges, and the square interior gives one face.
For each oriented edge, count its appearances with sign in \(aba^{-1}b^{-1}\). This abelian boundary computation does not make the attaching loop itself trivial in the rose.
Use \(H_1=\ker d_1/\operatorname{im}d_2\), checking the endpoint boundary of each loop edge and the exponent sums of the face word.
Use the filtration \(\mathbb RP^{k-1}\subset\mathbb RP^k\); the complement contributes one open \(k\)-cell at each stage.
Check the low-dimensional case \(d_2=2\), then use the two hemispherical contributions to distinguish even and odd indices consistently.
All degree-one chains are cycles, but the attached two-cell contributes the subgroup \(2\mathbb Z\) of boundaries.
Over \(\mathbb Z\), multiplication by two is injective. There are no three-cells, so compute the top kernel without introducing mod-two coefficients.
At degree three the outgoing differential is zero and there is no incoming degree-four map; both facts are needed for the top homology group.
Place the three generators in degrees two, one, and zero; the attaching degree belongs to \(d_2\), while the loop edge has zero vertex boundary.
Quotient the degree-one cycle group by \(m\mathbb Z\); for negative \(m\), the subgroup and cyclic group depend only on \(|m|\).
Use \(n\ge1\) and a nonzero attaching degree \(m\) for the stated Moore-space homology pattern; identify the only two positive-dimensional chain groups.
Compute the kernel and cokernel of \(\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{m}\mathbb Z\). The assertion that other reduced groups vanish uses \(m\ne0\).
Use the standard cellular differentials in degrees three, two, and one: zero, multiplication by \(p\), and zero; keep the integral coefficients fixed.
The surface relator is a product of commutators, each with zero exponent sum in every generator; combine this with the common vertex of all one-cells.
For a connected closed orientable surface, the top cellular cycle has no incoming three-dimensional boundaries; retain connectedness when counting its generators.
Count cells with sign \((-1)^n\) in each dimension and require a finite CW complex for the unqualified finite alternating sum.
Use the induced maps on \((X^n,X^{n-1})\to(Y^n,Y^{n-1})\); naturality of the connecting maps gives the commuting differential squares.
Write the triple \(X^{n-2}\subset X^{n-1}\subset X^n\) and identify the degree-lowering connecting map between its two consecutive cellular chain groups.
The quotient identifies chains differing by a chain supported in \(A\); it does not require every simplex representative to avoid \(A\).
Replace \(c\) by \(c+a\), with \(a\in C_n(A)\), and verify that their boundaries differ by a chain in \(C_{n-1}(A)\).
A relative cycle may have a nonzero absolute boundary, provided that boundary lies in \(C_{n-1}(A)\); apply the quotient differential when testing cycles.
There are no singular simplices with nonempty standard domain mapping to the empty set, so its chain groups vanish.
Every absolute chain is identified with zero in the quotient by the same chain group; inspect the resulting zero complex in each degree.
Use the inclusion and quotient maps and verify injectivity, surjectivity, and image equal to kernel degree by degree.
To construct the new arrow, lift a quotient cycle to an absolute chain and take its boundary; that boundary lies in the subspace chain complex.
Track degrees on the connecting arrow: it starts at relative degree \(n\) and ends at subspace degree \(n-1\).
Name the inclusion-induced map \(i_*\) and quotient-induced map \(j_*\); a class is killed by \(j_*\) precisely when it lies in \(\operatorname{im}i_*\).
Choose \(c\in C_n(X)\) with \(\partial c\in C_{n-1}(A)\); replacing the relative representative must change \(\partial c\) only by an \(A\)-boundary.
Use \(D^n/S^{n-1}\cong S^n\) for this CW pair, or use the reduced pair sequence to handle the two endpoints when \(n=1\).
Require a nonempty CW subcomplex \(A\) for the usual quotient statement and use reduced homology of the quotient, especially in degree zero.
Write the hypothesis \(\overline Z\subset\operatorname{int}_X(A)\) and identify the inclusion of pairs that induces the claimed isomorphism.
Apply excision to reduce a cell calculation to \((D^n,S^{n-1})\), checking the interior condition before removing any subset.
Distinguish the three quotient complexes \(C_*(A)/C_*(B)\), \(C_*(X)/C_*(B)\), and \(C_*(X)/C_*(A)\).
Apply the homology long exact sequence to \(0\to C_*(A,B)\to C_*(X,B)\to C_*(X,A)\to0\), retaining the degree shift.
Set \((X,A,B)=(X^n,X^{n-1},X^{n-2})\); the triple connecting arrow has target \(H_{n-1}(X^{n-1},X^{n-2})\).
Collapse the old subcomplex so that the newly attached disks become a wedge of \(n\)-spheres; orient the disks to choose the relative generators.
The relative cellular complex has no generators outside degree \(n\); distinguish this relative vanishing from the absolute homology of \(X\).
Examine the cokernel of \(H_0(A)\to H_0(X)\); the inclusion must hit the generator for every path component of \(X\).
Apply the pair sequence with \(A=\{x_0\}\); the map on \(H_0\) is injective, explaining why the degree-one case also works.
Require \(f(A)\subset B\), so the absolute chain map carries the subcomplex being quotiented out into the corresponding target subcomplex.
For the connecting square, compare \(\partial(f_\#c)\) with \(f_\#(\partial c)\) on a lifted relative cycle.
A homotopy of pairs must carry \(A\times I\) into \(B\); this is the condition that allows the prism operator to descend to relative chains.
Write \(P_n:C_n\to D_{n+1}\), then verify that both \(\partial^D_{n+1}P_n\) and \(P_{n-1}\partial^C_n\) have the same domain and target as \(g_n-f_n\).
A differential lowers degree by one, so its composite with the desired operator must have degree zero to compare two chain maps.
Substitute \(\partial z=0\) into the chain-homotopy equation and identify the explicit chain whose boundary is the difference of image cycles.
Apply the homotopy to the prism \(\sigma\times\operatorname{id}_I\) over each singular simplex, using an oriented triangulation of that prism.
A prism over an \(n\)-simplex has dimension \(n+1\); choose compatible orientations so internal faces cancel when the pieces are added.
Separate the top and bottom faces from the side faces of the prism; their signs determine the endpoint difference and the \(P\partial\) term.
Combine the prism identity with the cycle argument; the conclusion is equality of induced maps, not necessarily equality of chain maps.
Apply homology to both homotopy-inverse composites and use functoriality to obtain two actual inverse homomorphisms.
Use reduced rather than ordinary homology: the point has zero reduced groups but has an ordinary degree-zero copy of \(\mathbb Z\).
A contraction supplies paths from all points to its terminal point; use the path-component interpretation of \(H_0\).
Let \(i\) be the inclusion and \(r\) the deformation retraction; apply homology to \(ri=\operatorname{id}\) and \(ir\simeq\operatorname{id}\).
From \(r_*i_*=\operatorname{id}\), apply \(r_*\) to an equation \(i_*(a)=0\); this identifies the kernel of \(i_*\).
For a target class \(a\), the element \(i_*(a)\) provides an explicit preimage under \(r_*\).
A constant map factors through a point, whose reduced homology vanishes. Ordinary \(H_0\) would require a different statement.
Choose oriented generators of the top homology groups for \(n\ge1\); the multiplication integer is the degree and is unchanged when the induced homomorphism is unchanged.
Use the nonzero reduced top class of the sphere; for \(S^0\), reduced degree-zero homology also detects the failure of contractibility.
Compare \(T^2\) with \(S^1\vee S^1\vee S^2\): their integral homology groups agree, but their fundamental groups are respectively abelian and nonabelian.
Vanishing reduced homology does not test nonabelian fundamental-group information; a contractibility argument would need more than all homology classes vanishing.
State the condition \(H(A\times I)\subset B\) throughout the homotopy, not merely that the endpoint maps preserve the subspaces.
For a simplex lying in \(A\), its entire homotopy prism maps into \(B\); hence the operator preserves the subcomplexes being quotiented out.
Replace the CW model by a homotopy-equivalent simpler one and compute there; do not assume a smaller complex is valid solely from matching cell counts.
Distinguish a homotopy of continuous maps from a degree-raising algebraic operator on singular chains satisfying the boundary equation.
Follow the algebraic equation \(g-f=\partial P+P\partial\) to VIII/22, where its symmetry, composition, and equivalence properties are studied independently of spaces.
For finite CW complexes, apply Euler--Poincare to the homology ranks; the finiteness condition makes the alternating sum an ordinary finite sum.
Specify that \(c_n\) counts \(n\)-cells and that only finitely many cells occur; signs depend on cell dimension, not on orientations.
Count simplices of every dimension, including vertices, exactly once; do not count each simplex again every time it is a face of a larger one.
Use the cell decomposition with one degree-zero generator and no positive-dimensional cells to fix the normalization.
Compare the endpoint-and-edge count with the homology of a point; these two calculations should agree although the cell counts differ.
Track the contribution of the common vertex and the loop edge separately; the endpoint identification does not remove the vertex cell.
The top cell contributes with sign \((-1)^n\); check both parity cases and treat \(S^0\) as two zero-cells.
All terms above dimension one vanish. The formula does not require graph connectedness, although rank formulas may.
Solve the connected-graph rank equation for \(V-E\); the connectedness assumption supplies the single degree-zero homology generator.
For a finite tree, use \(E=V-1\), or compare its homology with a point; avoid an undefined infinite alternating count.
Insert the surface's one vertex, \(2g\) edges, and one face with their respective dimension signs.
Pair consecutive terms in \(1-1+1-\cdots+(-1)^n\); determine whether an unpaired term remains.
Use ranks of integral homology, equivalently dimensions after tensoring with \(\mathbb Q\), and require finite CW type for this finite formula.
A finite cyclic group becomes zero after tensoring with \(\mathbb Q\); its order is not a Betti number.
Compute the alternating homology rank sum for either CW decomposition; singular homology depends on the space rather than its particular cells.
A homotopy equivalence induces isomorphisms in each homology degree, hence preserves every rank appearing in the finite Euler sum.
Ordinary homology has one degree-zero generator and no positive-degree classes; reduced acyclicity alone is not a proof of contractibility.
The cell sets of a finite disjoint union are disjoint in every dimension; add their signed contributions before simplifying.
Choose basepoints that are zero-cells; gluing identifies two such cells as one, so compare the count with disjoint-union additivity.
A product of cells of dimensions \(i\) and \(j\) contributes sign \((-1)^{i+j}=(-1)^i(-1)^j\); factor the finite double sum.
Write the torus as a finite product of circles and apply multiplicativity, noting why the restriction \(n\ge1\) excludes the point.
For compatible finite subcomplexes, a cell in \(A\cap B\) has been counted twice; subtract its contribution exactly once.
Only the count in dimension \(n\) changes. The attaching degree can affect homology without changing this Euler increment.
Lift the CW structure from the base and count \(d\) copies of every open cell, then take the same alternating sum upstairs.
Rank calculations discard torsion and maps; the next machinery retains chain homotopies, cone differentials, and coefficient-change information that Euler characteristic cannot see.
For the identity discussed in the solution, write \(s_n:C_n\to D_{n+1}\) and check the types of both terms comparing \(g_n\) and \(f_n\).
A differential has degree \(-1\); choose the degree of \(s\) so that \(\partial s+s\partial\) has degree zero.
To compare a chain map with itself, substitute \(g=f\) and test the zero operator in every degree.
Negate the entire equation \(g-f=\partial s+s\partial\); this reverses the endpoint order without changing the degrees.
Add the equations for \(g-f\) and \(h-g\); the middle chain map cancels and the operators add.
For a cycle \(z\), the summand \(s\partial z\) vanishes; identify the chain whose boundary is \(g(z)-f(z)\).
Two cycles define the same homology class precisely when their difference is a boundary; apply this to the images in the preceding identity.
To write \(f=\partial s+s\partial\), take a homotopy from zero to \(f\); reversing its direction negates \(s\) under this chapter's sign convention.
Apply the null-homotopy equation to an arbitrary cycle and exhibit an explicit boundary representing its image under \(f\).
For a chain map \(u:D\to E\), test \(us\); use \(\partial_Eu=u\partial_D\) to move the differential past \(u\).
For a chain map \(v:B\to C\), test \(sv\); use the commuting differential equation for \(v\) in the second summand.
Specify maps in both directions and homotopies of both composites to the relevant identities; do not require the composites to be literally equal.
Apply homology to each composite of the proposed homotopy inverses; chain homotopy turns those composites into identity homomorphisms.
Triangulate \(\Delta^n\times I\) and apply the topological homotopy; internal face cancellation produces the degree-raising prism operator.
Choose bases and check the dimensions of \(D^D_{n+1}S_n\) and \(S_{n-1}D^C_n\); both must match the matrix of \(g_n-f_n\).
Apply each homotopy to its own summand; an input with finite support still has finite support after this componentwise operation.
Use the graded Hom differential on degree-zero chain maps and degree-one operators; compare \(g-f\) with the differential image of \(s\).
Substitute \(|s|=1\) into \(\delta(T)=\partial_D T-(-1)^{|T|}T\partial_C\) before simplifying the sign.
Require the homotopy operator to carry the distinguished source subcomplex into the distinguished target subcomplex, so it is well defined on quotient chains.
View the augmentation as an extra differential in degree zero; include the bottom-degree compatibility rather than checking only positive degrees.
Compare two choices by an explicit operator \(s\); equality of the resulting homology maps follows from the boundary of \(s(z)\) for each cycle.
When \(g-f=0\), a degree-one zero operator satisfies the homotopy equation even when the chain groups themselves are nonzero.
For a comparison between complexes, distinguish chain-homotopy equivalence from chain isomorphism; the elementary identity two-term complex is equivalent to zero but not isomorphic to it.
Set one endpoint map to zero and the other to the identity, keeping track of the sign convention used when naming the contraction operator.
Check \(s_n:C_n\to C_{n+1}\) and verify \(\partial_{n+1}s_n+s_{n-1}\partial_n=\operatorname{id}_{C_n}\) in each degree.
Evaluate the contraction equation on a cycle; the resulting filling shows that every cycle represents the zero homology class.
When \(\partial z=0\), compute \(\partial s(z)\); the operator provides an explicit filling rather than just an existence argument.
Test the exact complex \(0\to\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/2\to0\); a contraction would force a splitting that does not exist.
Write \(C_n=B_n\oplus L_n\) with \(\partial:L_n\to B_{n-1}\) an isomorphism, and use its inverse on the boundary summand to define \(s\).
Choose a complement to each cycle subspace. Exactness identifies the differential on that complement with the boundary subspace one degree lower.
Send the lower copy of \(A\) back to the upper copy by the identity, set other components to zero, and verify the equation on both copies.
Choose a cone vertex and prepend it to an oriented simplex, with zero assigned to repeated-vertex simplices; include the augmented degree in the boundary check.
Ordinary degree-zero homology of a point is nonzero, so its identity cannot be null-homotopic; augmentation removes this obstruction.
For a chain map \(f:C\to D\), test \(fs\) as the null-homotopy operator and use that \(f\) commutes with differentials.
For a chain map \(f:D\to C\), test \(sf\), using the contraction on the target rather than on the source.
Take the direct sum of the degree-raising operators and check the identity separately on every summand, retaining finite support.
First isolate a unit boundary coefficient by compatible basis operations; then invert that unit to contract the paired generators and adjust neighboring maps.
A nonzero field element has an inverse, whereas an integer pivot such as two cannot be inverted over \(\mathbb Z\).
On an isolated two-term block with differential \(\pm1\), its inverse supplies the degree-raising contraction of that block.
For an isolated block \(\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{m}\mathbb Z\), compute the cokernel; a nonzero torsion class rules out a contraction.
Given a cycle \(z\), the certificate must produce the chain \(s(z)\) and verify its boundary is exactly \(z\).
Since \(\partial\) lowers degree, \(s\) must raise it for the two composites in the contraction equation to act in the original degree.
For a chain isomorphism \(u:C\to D\), conjugate the contraction to \(usu^{-1}\) and verify the identity on \(D\).
The only maps between a complex and zero compose to zero; the homotopy-inverse condition therefore says its identity is null-homotopic.
A topological contraction first compares the identity chain map with a map through a point; pass to the reduced or augmented model to eliminate the point's degree-zero class.
Check that \(s\) preserves each filtration level; an unfiltered contraction need not induce a valid contraction of the filtered objects.
For a contraction on the second tensor factor, test \(S(c\otimes d)=(-1)^{|c|}c\otimes s(d)\) and verify cancellation with the tensor differential.
Compare the two tests: an acyclic cone detects a quasi-isomorphism, while an explicit cone contraction detects the stronger chain-homotopy-equivalence condition.
The second summand is shifted: an element of \(C_{n-1}\) joins an element of \(D_n\) to make a cone chain of degree \(n\).
Check that \(f(c)\) and \(\partial_D d\) both lie in \(D_{n-1}\), while the second output lies in \(C_{n-2}\).
The shifted differential contributes \(-\partial_C\); trace this sign when applying the cone differential a second time.
Expand both components of \(d^2(d,c)\). The mixed first-component terms cancel precisely because \(\partial_D f=f\partial_C\).
An element originally in degree \(k\) of \(C\) occurs in degree \(k+1\) of \(C[1]\); use this to check the index direction.
Compare the projection \(\operatorname{Cone}(f)\to C[1]\) with the cone differential; the projected differential must have the same minus sign.
Use \(d\mapsto(d,0)\) for the inclusion and \((d,c)\mapsto c\) for the projection; verify exactness and the chain-map conditions.
Identify \(H_n(C[1])\) with \(H_{n-1}(C)\); lifting \(c\) as \((0,c)\) identifies the connecting arrow with the map induced by \(f\).
For the identity cone, test the degree-raising operator \(s(d,c)=(0,d)\) and compute \(ds+sd\) explicitly.
Set \(f=0\) in the differential; the two summands then have independent differentials, yielding a direct sum of complexes.
A quasi-isomorphism requires an isomorphism on every homology group, not a degreewise isomorphism of the chain groups.
Use exactness on both sides of \(H_n(\operatorname{Cone}(f))\) to relate its vanishing to injectivity and surjectivity of the neighboring \(H_*(f)\).
The long exact sequence proves only acyclicity. To obtain contractibility, use a chain-homotopy inverse and the homotopies as additional chain-level data.
An acyclic complex can be nonsplit over a general ring; a contraction supplies splittings and explicit fillings, not merely vanishing homology.
A strict chain inverse is also a chain-homotopy inverse with zero comparison homotopies; apply the stronger cone criterion.
For an inclusion \(i:A\hookrightarrow B\), use \((b,a)\mapsto[b]\) from the cone to \(B/A\) and examine its kernel to compare their homology.
Keep track of augmentation: ordinary chains of a nonempty contractible topological cone retain \(H_0\), whereas the algebraic cone of an identity is acyclic.
For a strictly commuting square \(vf=f'u\), apply \(v\) on the target summand and \(u\) on the shifted source summand; check the mixed term.
If \(vf-f'u=\partial h+h\partial\), test the corrected map \((d,c)\mapsto(vd+h(c),u(c))\) and verify its differential equation.
Both original complexes occupy degree zero, so the shifted source becomes degree one and the unshifted target remains degree zero.
The degree-zero outgoing differential is zero, while the incoming image is \(m\mathbb Z\); take that quotient over \(\mathbb Z\).
Compare the cokernel of multiplication by \(m\) with the cellular boundary of a degree-\(m\) attachment, accounting for the change in degree.
Write the cone inclusion and shifted projection explicitly; their associated long exact sequence explains the triangle pattern without treating it as a short exact sequence of four objects.
Tensor the displayed cone differential with the coefficient group. The cone formula persists, but tensoring need not preserve a quasi-isomorphism without suitable hypotheses.
Tensor the chain groups and differential first, then take kernels and images; tensoring the already-computed homology can miss an adjacent Tor contribution.
Use the chain isomorphism \(c\otimes n\mapsto nc\) from \(C_*(X)\otimes\mathbb Z\) to the integral chain complex.
The free integral chain generators become a basis over \(\mathbb F_p\); compute the differential as a linear map over that field.
Reduce every integer matrix entry in the same field, then recompute ranks and kernels there rather than reusing rational ranks.
The relevant two-term coefficient complex is \(G\xrightarrow{m}G\); both its kernel and cokernel may differ from their integral counterparts.
Replace the integer boundary coefficient two by its residue in \(\mathbb F_2\); this changes the kernel as well as the image.
There is one mod-two cellular generator in each degree zero, one, and two, and both differentials vanish in that field.
In degree \(n\), all chains are cycles and the incoming subgroup is \(mG\); compute the quotient in the chosen coefficient group.
At degree \(n+1\), there is no higher incoming chain group; cycles are exactly the elements of \(G\) annihilated by \(m\).
Use that the residue of \(m\) is nonzero in a field; invert it to determine both the kernel and cokernel.
When \(m\) is zero in \(\mathbb F_p\), the two-term differential is zero, so both adjacent chain groups contribute to homology.
Define \(n\otimes g\mapsto ng\) and its inverse \(g\mapsto1\otimes g\); verify they respect the tensor relations.
Tensor the presentation \(\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{m}\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/m\to0\) and use right exactness to identify its cokernel.
The tensor product is generated by \(1\otimes1\), annihilated by both \(m\) and \(n\); use their greatest common divisor to determine its order.
Tensor the injection \(\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{p}\mathbb Z\) with \(\mathbb Z/p\); its loss of injectivity illustrates the kernel recorded by Tor.
Singular chain groups are free, hence flat, so tensoring the short exact coefficient sequence remains exact in each chain degree.
Lift a quotient-coefficient cycle to a middle-coefficient chain, take its boundary, and identify the resulting class with coefficients in the leftmost group.
Lift a mod-\(p\) cycle to an integral chain \(c\); its boundary is divisible by \(p\), and \((\partial c)/p\) represents the integral connecting class.
A coefficient map \(\phi:G\to H\) gives \(\operatorname{id}\otimes\phi\) on chains; verify this commutes with the coefficient differentials.
Use the quotient singular chain complex, whose basis consists of simplices not wholly in \(A\), then tensor it with \(G\).
Use path connectedness for the singular-homology statement: augmentation identifies \(H_0(X;G)\) with \(G\), leaving a zero reduced kernel.
In characteristic two, \(-1=1\); oppositely oriented faces have the same coefficient, explaining why orientation obstructions change.
For a torsion element killed by nonzero \(m\), multiplication by \(m\) becomes invertible over \(\mathbb Q\); its tensor contribution vanishes.
Keep both degrees in view: tensor uses integral \(H_n\), while the correction uses integral \(H_{n-1}\).
Identify the left-hand map \(H_n(X;\mathbb Z)\otimes G\to H_n(X;G)\); the integral group is in the same degree as the requested coefficient homology.
The Tor correction uses the integral group one degree lower, \(H_{n-1}(X;\mathbb Z)\), rather than another copy of \(H_n\).
Distinguish a natural short exact sequence from a chosen splitting of that sequence; an abstract direct-sum isomorphism need not commute with induced maps.
Free abelian groups have zero first Tor with any coefficient group; apply this to the lower-degree integral homology term only.
Use the map \(n\otimes g\mapsto ng\) and inverse \(g\mapsto1\otimes g\) to identify the free rank-one contribution.
Resolve the free group \(\mathbb Z\) by itself in degree zero; there is no positive resolution homology from which Tor could arise.
Tensor the presentation of \(\mathbb Z/m\) and take the cokernel of multiplication by \(m\) on \(G\).
Use the same two-term free resolution, but now take the kernel of multiplication by \(m\), not its cokernel.
Compute \((\mathbb Z/n)/m(\mathbb Z/n)\); its order is the index of the image of multiplication by \(m\).
Solve \(mx=0\) in \(\mathbb Z/n\) and identify that cyclic subgroup; distinguish this kernel from the quotient used for the tensor term.
List integral \(H_2(\mathbb RP^2)=0\) and \(H_1(\mathbb RP^2)=\mathbb Z/2\); the zero tensor term does not force coefficient homology to vanish.
Compute \(\ker(2:\mathbb F_2\to\mathbb F_2)\) for the lower-degree torsion group and place its contribution in mod-two degree two.
For a Moore space, place \(G/mG\) in the torsion group's own degree and \(\ker(m:G\to G)\) in the next degree.
Multiplication by any nonzero integer is invertible on \(\mathbb Q\), so both cyclic torsion tensor terms and their Tor terms vanish.
Decompose finitely generated integral homology into free and torsion summands; rationalization preserves exactly one dimension per free generator.
For \(f:X\to Y\), use \(H_n(f)\otimes\operatorname{id}\) on the left and the induced Tor map from \(H_{n-1}(f)\) on the right.
For \(G\to G'\), compare the tensor and Tor functors in their coefficient argument, and keep the same integral homology groups.
Apply \(-\otimes G\) to \(0\to\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{m}\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/m\to0\); the two derived outputs are its kernel and cokernel.
Relative singular chains are free abelian on simplices not lying wholly in the subspace, so the free-chain UCT applies to that quotient complex.
Use the augmented complex and track the bottom degree separately; the reduced version removes the universal component contribution, not higher torsion.
Distribute tensor and Tor over the finite free-and-cyclic decomposition before combining the contributions to the short exact sequence.
Each cyclic summand divisible by \(p\) contributes one dimension, from both degree \(n\) tensor and degree \(n-1\) Tor, in addition to the free rank.
A splitting selects lifts of quotient elements into the middle group; explain why such a selection is extra data rather than part of the natural UCT maps.
For a product, replace the fixed coefficient group by the graded homology of a second complex and track total degrees in tensor and Tor sums.
In total degree \(n\), include every bidegree \((p,q)\) with \(p+q=n\); distinguish a graded direct sum from a single tensor factor.
For homogeneous \(c\in C_p\), use \(\partial(c\otimes d)=\partial c\otimes d+(-1)^p c\otimes\partial d\).
Expand the double differential; the two mixed terms have signs \((-1)^{p-1}\) and \((-1)^p\) and therefore cancel.
Compare \(C_*(X\times Y)\) with \(C_*(X)\otimes C_*(Y)\) by chain maps and chain homotopies, not by claiming their generators coincide.
The cross product combines representative cycles of dimensions \(p\) and \(q\); the tensor differential verifies their product has zero boundary.
Sum \(H_p(X)\otimes H_q(Y)\) over \(p+q=n\), including the degree-zero contributions from either factor.
A Tor term from degrees \(p,q\) contributes to degree \(p+q+1\); check this shift before computing a product's torsion.
Tensor over the coefficient field itself; vector spaces are flat, so no Tor correction remains in the field-coefficient formula.
In total degree one, list bidegrees \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) for the two circles and add their tensor contributions.
The top class comes from the product of the two degree-one circle generators, in bidegree \((1,1)\).
Choose which \(k\) circle factors contribute degree one while the others contribute degree zero; count those choices.
List bidegrees \((2,0)\) and \((0,2)\); each supplies an independent copy of \(\mathbb Z\), while the \((2,2)\) class lies in degree four.
For a nonempty contractible factor, the projection is a homotopy equivalence; alternatively use its sole ordinary degree-zero homology group in Künneth.
Locate torsion groups in both factors and test their common prime divisors; the resulting Tor class sits one degree above the corresponding tensor total degree.
Use the resolution of \(\mathbb Z/2\) and compute the kernel of multiplication by two on the second \(\mathbb Z/2\).
For torsion in Moore degrees \(r,s\), the mixed tensor contribution occurs in \(r+s\) and the mixed Tor contribution in \(r+s+1\), both governed by \(\gcd(m,n)\).
For maps of both spaces, check that the cross product obeys \((f\times g)_*(a\times b)=f_*(a)\times g_*(b)\).
The exact sequence has natural maps, but identifying its middle term with the sum of tensor and Tor terms requires a generally nonnatural splitting.
Over a field, take dimensions of each tensor summand and add over \(p+q=n\); finite-type assumptions make these ordinary finite Betti-number sums.
Multiply the two generating functions and identify the coefficient of \(t^n\) with the convolution formula for product Betti numbers.
The circle contributes \(1+t\); multiply one copy for each circle factor and compare coefficients using the binomial theorem.
For finite CW type, evaluate the product of Poincare polynomials at \(t=-1\) to recover the Euler-product formula.
Use the homotopies between each composite and the relevant identity to show the induced homology maps are inverse, even though the chain maps are not strict inverses.
The diagonal \(X\to X\times X\) turns an external cohomology product into an internal one; retain degrees and signs when passing to the cup-product ring.
A degree-\(n\) cochain assigns values in \(G\) linearly to degree-\(n\) chains; for infinitely many free generators, this Hom group is a product of coefficient groups.
